t: Pan-Africanism, born among Black thinkers of the Caribbean, North America and Britain, held that Africans and people of African descent share a common history and destiny.
From the London conference of 1900 to the Manchester congress of 1945 it moved from appeals for fair treatment to demands for the independence of Africa.
Leaders such as Kwame Nkrumah called for a united Africa; the new states founded the Organisation of African Unity in 1963 instead, and the African Union in 2002.
dyk: The words “the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the colour-line”, famous from W. E. B. Du Bois’s The Souls of Black Folk (1903), had already appeared in the address he drafted for the London conference of 1900.
ev: Henry Sylvester Williams’s Pan-African Conference meets in London; W. E. B. Du Bois drafts its address
Marcus Garvey founds the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica
Du Bois’s first Pan-African Congress meets in Paris during the peace conference
Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia unites Africans and the diaspora in protest
The Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester demands independence for Africa
Ghana becomes independent under Kwame Nkrumah; Accra hosts the All-African People’s Conference
Thirty-two independent states found the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa
The African Union replaces the Organisation of African Unity

f.where: Arose among people of African descent in the Caribbean, the United States and Britain; spread to West Africa and then across the continent
f.period: From the Pan-African Conference in London in 1900 to the present: congresses in 1900–1945, independence from 1957, the Organisation of African Unity from 1963 and the African Union from 2002
f.figures: Henry Sylvester Williams, W. E. B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey, George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere
f.outcome: Inspired Africa’s independence movements and founded the Organisation of African Unity, succeeded by the African Union; continental political union was never achieved
